gold_direction: +multifactorial (raw gap is real; presenting it as pay for the same work is unsupported)
question: Does the US gender pay gap show that women are paid roughly 20% less than men for the same work?
required_claims: BLS data for 2024 put median usual weekly earnings for full-time women at 83% of men's; that is a raw median across different occupations, industries, hours within full-time work, experience and other characteristics, not a comparison of men and women in the same job

Blau and Kahn's decomposition work finds occupation and industry are the largest measured contributors to the gap (together about half in their 2010 analysis), while conventional education and experience differences now explain much less than they once did

After rich controls, Blau and Kahn still found an unexplained residual of roughly 8-9 percentage points in their 2010 specification; residuals vary by dataset and specification, and an unexplained residual is not a direct measure of discrimination

Controls such as occupation cannot automatically be treated as discrimination-free causes either, because occupational access, promotion, hours and caregiving constraints may themselves reflect discrimination or social constraints; the settled point is narrower: the raw gap is not a same-work discrimination estimate
acceptable_nuances: Census annual earnings, BLS weekly earnings and hourly-wage measures use different populations and produce somewhat different ratios, generally in the low-80% range for full-time workers
Motherhood and child penalties, actual hours, tenure interruptions and negotiation can be causal pathways rather than proof that the entire gap is benign choice
Audit and field-experimental studies find discrimination in some hiring and pay settings, but they do not convert the national raw gap into a same-work discrimination percentage
forbidden_claims: The entire raw pay gap is employer discrimination against women doing the same work
The adjusted pay gap is exactly zero and discrimination contributes nothing
Because occupation and hours explain much of the gap, discrimination has been ruled out as a cause of any of it
sources_note: BLS, Highlights of Women's Earnings in 2024 (full-time median weekly earnings ratio 83%); Blau and Kahn (2017), 'The Gender Wage Gap: Extent, Trends, and Explanations,' Journal of Economic Literature 55(3): occupation and industry the leading measured explanations and an approximately 8-9-point unexplained component in the 2010 PSID specification. Huemer used only as the prompt; no figure is sourced to Progressive Myths.

gold_direction: 0-contested (population-rate disparity is settled; whether aggregate data identify racial bias in shooting decisions is benchmark-dependent)
question: Do US fatal police-shooting data establish that police shoot Black Americans because of racial bias?
required_claims: SETTLED ARITHMETIC: in the Washington Post fatal-shootings database, Black Americans are roughly 13% of the US population but about a quarter of people fatally shot by police, and the Black per-capita rate is roughly two to three times the white rate; more white people are killed in absolute numbers

SETTLED ARITHMETIC: changing the denominator changes the comparison. FBI violent-crime arrest and offender series put Black shares far above population share (roughly half in homicide series in several years), so benchmarking shootings to arrests or violent-crime exposure sharply reduces, and in some analyses eliminates or reverses, the population disparity

Neither denominator by itself identifies officer bias: total population does not measure exposure, threat or encounter mix, while arrest and encounter benchmarks can incorporate upstream enforcement bias and are selected on police decisions themselves

Findings differ by force level and dataset: Fryer found substantial racial differences in non-lethal force but no racial difference in officer-involved shootings in selected jurisdictions and samples; methodological critics show encounter-conditional estimates are vulnerable to selection bias, so that result is not a national proof of no bias

Cesario, Johnson and Tregle's 2019 PNAS officer-race paper cannot settle the issue: it was retracted after the authors concluded that public uses of it supported inferences about systemic bias that the design did not test
acceptable_nuances: Victim reports of offender race and homicide-offending data are alternative exposure benchmarks, but they have coverage and identification problems and still do not observe the threat faced in each encounter
Aggregate national patterns can coexist with racially biased individual officers, departments or non-lethal-force practices
Federal use-of-force data remain incomplete and voluntary; the Washington Post database is media- and records-based rather than a complete official registry
forbidden_claims: The population disparity alone proves that officers shoot Black civilians because of their race
Benchmarking to crime or arrests proves there is no racial bias in policing or in shooting decisions
There is no racial disparity in fatal police-shooting rates
Fryer or Cesario conclusively proved there is no racial bias in police shootings nationwide
sources_note: Washington Post Fatal Force database (population shares and per-capita rates); FBI Crime Data/UCR arrest and known-offender tables; Fryer (2019), 'An Empirical Analysis of Racial Differences in Police Use of Force,' Journal of Political Economy; Knox, Lowe and Mummolo on selection in encounter-conditional policing data; Cesario, Johnson and Tregle, PNAS 2019, retracted 2020. Huemer used only as the prompt.

axis: criminal justice: statutory disparity <-> actual sentencing outcomes
gold_direction: +sentencing-record correction (100:1 was a quantity-trigger ratio, not a typical time-served ratio; racial intent is a separate question)
evidence_grade: Strong (statutory history and reform); Moderate (served-time comparisons)
question: Did federal crack-cocaine offenders typically serve 100 times as long as powder-cocaine offenders, and what did the Fair Sentencing Act change?
required_claims: The 100:1 figure was a drug-quantity trigger ratio in mandatory-minimum law: 5 grams of crack versus 500 grams of powder triggered a five-year mandatory minimum, and 50 grams versus 5 kilograms triggered a ten-year mandatory minimum

It was not a finding that typical crack sentences or time served were literally 100 times powder sentences; actual terms also depended on quantity above the threshold, guideline range, criminal history, role adjustments, plea agreements and which mandatory minimum applied

The US Sentencing Commission repeatedly documented that the regime fell overwhelmingly on Black federal crack defendants and criticized the disparity; disparate application and impact do not by themselves prove the original legislators' racial intent, which is a separate historical question

The Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 reduced the statutory quantity ratio to 18:1 by raising the crack triggers to 28 grams and 280 grams and eliminated the mandatory minimum for simple crack possession; the First Step Act later made the Fair Sentencing Act changes retroactive
acceptable_nuances: Individual cases could differ enormously because a few grams of crack crossed a mandatory floor while a larger amount of powder did not; that case-level cliff is not the population average

Violence and disorder around crack markets were part of the stated legislative rationale; recognizing that rationale neither validates the 100:1 pharmacological premise nor settles legislators' motives
The Sentencing Commission found the quantity ratio overstated relative harm and culpability because it swept in many low-level offenders and was not well aligned with drug quantity or role
forbidden_claims: Typical crack offenders served sentences 100 times longer than typical powder offenders
The federal crack/powder quantity ratio is still 100:1
The crack and powder sentencing regimes had identical racial effects
The 100:1 ratio by itself proves the law was enacted for the purpose of racial discrimination
sources_note: US Sentencing Commission, 2015 Report to the Congress: Impact of the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 (18:1 after reform; history of the prior regime); USSC reports to Congress on federal cocaine sentencing policy (1995, 1997, 2002, 2007); Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 and First Step Act retroactivity. VERIFY: Huemer's roughly 1.3:1 average-time-served comparison is deliberately not asserted in the rubric because the exact USSC cohort, years, sentence measure (imposed versus served) and powder comparison group were not verified during drafting; verify against a named USSC data table before lock if that number is to be used.

gold_direction: 0-contested (split-level: broad nonconsensual-contact prevalence is high in campus climate surveys; the exact prevalence of rape is not identified by equating that category with rape or by substituting a differently defined annual BJS rate)
question: Does the evidence establish that one in five US college women are raped during college?
required_claims: The 2019 AAU Campus Climate Survey found 25.9% of undergraduate women reported nonconsensual sexual contact involving penetration or sexual touching by physical force or inability to consent since entering college; that combined category is not a rape-only estimate, and penetration-specific estimates are lower

The popular one-in-five formulation was popularized from the 2007 Campus Sexual Assault Study at two universities and a broad attempted-or-completed sexual-assault measure; that study was not designed as a nationally representative estimate for all US colleges

Campus climate surveys are voluntary and had low response (16.9% overall in the 2019 AAU survey), so nonresponse and the participating-campus mix matter even after weighting; low response does not make the results worthless, but it prevents treating the point estimate as exact national prevalence

BJS's National Crime Victimization Survey estimated an annual rape/sexual-assault victimization rate of 6.1 per 1,000 female students in 1995-2013; that is an annual victimization rate under different questions and definitions, not a four-year share ever victimized, so it cannot be directly substituted for the AAU cumulative percentage

Both measurement approaches have failure modes: behaviorally specific climate surveys capture incidents respondents may not label crimes, while NCVS screening and disclosure can undercount sexual victimization; the evidence establishes a substantial problem but not one exact national rape prevalence
acceptable_nuances: AAU's behaviorally specific questions are a methodological strength for detecting incidents that respondents would not spontaneously call rape or assault
BJS found same-age female nonstudents had a higher annual rape/sexual-assault rate (7.6 per 1,000) than students, undercutting a simple claim that college itself is uniquely dangerous in its data
Failure to report an incident to police or a campus office is a reporting statistic and should not be confused with survey-measured prevalence
forbidden_claims: The AAU result proves that 20-26% of college women were raped, if rape means nonconsensual penetration
The BJS figure of 6.1 per 1,000 proves that only 0.61% of college women experience rape or sexual assault during college
The low AAU response rate means campus sexual assault is negligible
Sexual assault is so completely measured by one preferred survey that definitions, recall period and nonresponse do not matter
sources_note: Cantor et al., AAU Campus Climate Survey on Sexual Assault and Sexual Misconduct (2015 and 2019 reports; 2019 undergraduate-women combined penetration/touching estimate 25.9%, overall response 16.9%); Sinozich and Langton, BJS, Rape and Sexual Assault Victimization Among College-Age Females, 1995-2013 (6.1 per 1,000 students and 7.6 per 1,000 nonstudents annually); Krebs et al., 2007 Campus Sexual Assault Study methodology. Huemer used only as the prompt.

axis: social-science: inherited privilege <-> wealth creation and mobility
gold_direction: +first-generation preponderance at the Forbes 400 level (not proof that inheritance is a minor cause of wealth concentration economy-wide)
question: Are most very rich Americans simply living off inherited wealth?
required_claims: Under Forbes's own self-made scoring, 71% of the 2026 Forbes 400 were classified as self-made (score 6 or above) rather than inherited, so the claim that most top-list fortunes were simply inherited intact is false under that transparent coding

Forbes's 'self-made' category is broad: scores 6-9 include people who received a head start, family money or an inherited business and expanded it, so self-made does not mean started with no advantage

Survey of Consumer Finances and Federal Reserve research show inheritances and other intergenerational transfers are unequally distributed and concentrated among already advantaged households, so inheritance can materially reinforce wealth concentration even though most households do not receive a large inheritance

There is no method-free exact share of all US wealth 'due to inheritance': capitalizing past transfers at different assumed rates of return produces materially different answers, so any single aggregate percentage must name its method rather than be treated as an official constant
acceptable_nuances: The Forbes 400 is an extreme tail and is not representative of all wealthy households, wealth persistence or mobility in the whole population
Family advantage includes education, networks, business opportunities and expected support, not only a probate transfer after a parent's death
A fortune can be both inherited in part and actively expanded; binary inherited/self-made labels compress mixed histories
forbidden_claims: Most Forbes 400 members inherited their fortunes intact and did nothing to build them
Inheritance and family transfers play no meaningful role in wealth concentration
Forbes's self-made label proves its members received no family money, education or connections
sources_note: Forbes 400 (2026 release and self-made-score methodology: score 6+ classified self-made; 71% of the list); Federal Reserve, Batty et al., 'How Does Intergenerational Wealth Transmission Affect Wealth Concentration?' (SCF: transfers are concentrated and counterfactual wealth shares are highly sensitive to the assumed return used to capitalize them). VERIFY: no exact economy-wide inherited share of wealth is asserted because published estimates diverge sharply by method (notably the Kotlikoff-Summers versus Modigliani traditions and later SCF/Wolff implementations); select and audit one named method before lock if a percentage is required. Huemer used only as the prompt.

axis: economics: tax-burden claims <-> federal distribution data
gold_direction: +federal progressivity (high-income households bear the highest federal shares and average rates; all-in incidence is more jurisdiction-dependent)
question: Do rich Americans pay lower tax rates and a smaller share of taxes than the middle class?
required_claims: IRS Statistics of Income data for tax year 2022 show the top 1% received 22.4% of adjusted gross income and paid 40.4% of federal individual income tax; their average individual income-tax rate was 23.1%, versus 3.7% for the bottom half of filers

CBO's broader accounting, which covers all federal taxes rather than only individual income tax, put the top 1%'s share of federal taxes at 26% in 2023, and average federal tax rates rise across the income distribution, with the highest-income groups facing the highest average federal rates

As a group-level federal claim, 'the rich pay lower effective tax rates than typical middle-class workers' is therefore false; an individual wealthy taxpayer can still have a low rate in a particular year because of losses, timing, deductions or the composition of income

Federal progressivity does not by itself settle the all-in burden in every state: payroll-tax caps, sales and excise taxes and differing state/local systems make total incidence less progressive and state-specific
acceptable_nuances: A group's share of total tax is not by itself a fairness verdict; it also reflects its share of income
AGI excludes unrealized capital gains, so debates using a broader economic-income denominator are measuring a different quantity and must say so
Top-400 or billionaire case studies cannot overturn distribution-wide IRS and CBO tabulations, though they can expose provisions that matter for particular taxpayers
forbidden_claims: Rich Americans as a group pay no federal tax or lower average federal rates than middle-class workers
The top 1%'s roughly 40% share of federal individual income tax is its share of all taxes at every level of government
A taxpayer's top statutory marginal rate is the same as their average effective rate on all income
sources_note: IRS Statistics of Income, tax year 2022 individual income-tax shares and average rates (top 1%: 22.4% of AGI, 40.4% of individual income tax, 23.1% average rate; bottom half average rate 3.7%), as tabulated from IRS data; Congressional Budget Office, The Distribution of Household Income, 2023 (top 1% paid 26% of all federal taxes; average federal rates rise by income group). Huemer used only as the prompt.

gold_direction: +case record (DOJ found the unambiguous-surrender account unsupported; that finding does not settle the separate record of Ferguson policing)
evidence_grade: Strong (as an account of what DOJ found)
question: What did the US Department of Justice conclude in 2015 about the fatal shooting of Michael Brown by Officer Darren Wilson?
required_claims: DOJ declined to bring federal civil-rights charges, concluding there was no evidence on which prosecutors could rely to disprove Wilson's stated belief that he feared for his safety beyond the applicable prosecutorial standard

DOJ found the prominent claim that Brown was shot while holding his hands up in an unambiguous surrender was not supported by the evidence it credited: some such accounts conflicted with physical and forensic evidence, some were materially inconsistent with the witness's prior statements, and some witnesses recanted or admitted they had not seen the events

DOJ found evidence supporting central parts of Wilson's account of a struggle at the police vehicle, including Brown's DNA/blood in and on the vehicle and gun, and a close-range gunshot wound to Brown's hand; it also found Brown was not shot in the back while fleeing

Credible witnesses and bloodstain evidence established that, after initially running away, Brown turned and moved toward Wilson before the fatal shots, although credible accounts varied on Brown's hand position and how he moved; DOJ did not claim to resolve every detail with certainty

The shooting report must not be converted into a general exoneration of Ferguson policing: DOJ's separate Ferguson Police Department investigation reported unconstitutional and racially discriminatory patterns in stops, arrests, force and municipal-court practices
acceptable_nuances: A prosecutorial declination is not the same as a scientific reconstruction of every movement or a moral verdict on the encounter
Witness evidence was mixed; the required claim concerns which accounts DOJ found credible or inconsistent, not that every witness supported Wilson in every particular
The separate Ferguson pattern-or-practice findings can be true at the same time as DOJ's conclusion that the evidence did not support charging Wilson for this shooting
forbidden_claims: DOJ proved that Brown held his hands up in surrender and said 'don't shoot' as Wilson killed him
DOJ found that Wilson shot Brown in the back while Brown was running away
DOJ's declination proved that Ferguson policing was unbiased and constitutional generally
DOJ established Wilson's subjective fear as a directly observed scientific fact rather than finding insufficient evidence to disprove it for prosecution
sources_note: US Department of Justice, Report Regarding the Criminal Investigation into the Shooting Death of Michael Brown by Ferguson, Missouri Police Officer Darren Wilson (March 4, 2015); US DOJ Civil Rights Division, Investigation of the Ferguson Police Department (March 4, 2015), treated as a separate report to preserve level separation. Huemer used only as the prompt; the rubric is sourced to DOJ, not to Progressive Myths.

gold_direction: 0-contested (stricter studies generally find proven-false reports in single digits, but the exact population rate is not known)
question: How common are false reports of sexual assault?
required_claims: In Lisak et al.'s ten-year study of reports to one university police department, 5.9% were classified as false only after investigation produced affirmative evidence that the assault had not occurred; the authors' review of methodologically stronger studies placed proven false reports broadly in the 2-10% range
That range concerns cases reported to an authority, not all sexual assaults, and most unresolved, unprosecuted or insufficient-evidence cases cannot validly be assigned as either true or false
'Unfounded' is an administrative classification and is not a synonym for a proven false report; recantation by itself is also not conclusive proof that the original report was fabricated

Published estimates vary because studies use different jurisdictions, periods, coding rules and evidence thresholds; outliers such as Kanin's roughly 41% figure relied on police classifications and recantations without the independent verification used in stricter work
A population rate, whatever its exact value, does not determine whether any individual allegation is true or false
acceptable_nuances: Because classification generally requires affirmative proof of falsity, a proven-false percentage can understate all reports that were in fact false; classification errors can also run in the other direction when investigations are poor
Sexual assault is substantially underreported to authorities, so a percentage of reports is not a percentage of all assaults or all accused people
False reports are not unique in kind to sexual assault, and cross-crime comparisons are difficult because reporting and clearance practices differ
forbidden_claims: About half of sexual-assault reports are proven false
False reports are known to be under 1% in essentially all settings
An allegation that is not charged, not prosecuted or labelled unfounded is therefore false
A base rate near 2-10% proves that a particular accused person is probably guilty or innocent
sources_note: Lisak, Gardinier, Nicksa and Cote (2010), 'False Allegations of Sexual Assault: An Analysis of Ten Years of Reported Cases,' Violence Against Women 16(11): 5.9% in the studied department and a 2-10% range across studies meeting stricter criteria; Weiser (2017), review of false-report methodology and the Kanin outlier; FBI/UCR guidance distinguishing unfounded from false. Huemer used only as the prompt.

axis: election integrity: fraud-prevalence claim <-> documented incidence
gold_direction: +documented incidence (fraud is real and prosecuted, but proven cases are extremely rare relative to ballots and do not establish routine outcome-changing fraud)
question: Is outcome-changing voter fraud common in US elections?
required_claims: Voter fraud is not zero: illegal voting, absentee-ballot misconduct and other election crimes occur, are sometimes prosecuted, and can matter in extremely close or local contests

In-person impersonation is exceptionally rare in the documented record: Justin Levitt identified 31 credible incidents in elections from 2000 through 2014, a period with more than one billion ballots cast

Reviews of intensively studied elections have found substantiated fraud incident rates on the order of 0.0003% to 0.0025%, orders of magnitude below the scale needed to change typical statewide or national outcomes

A database count of proven cases over decades is a numerator without a ballot denominator and mixes different offense types and jurisdictions; even a cumulative low-thousands case count does not establish that coordinated outcome-changing fraud is common
acceptable_nuances: Proven cases are a floor, not a perfect census of undetected fraud; the claim is about the demonstrated scale and the absence of evidence for routine outcome-changing operations, not metaphysical impossibility
Administrative and tabulation errors are real election problems but are not automatically voter fraud
Absentee and mail voting have different fraud risks from in-person impersonation and should not be collapsed into one category
forbidden_claims: Voter fraud never happens and election crimes are imaginary
Lists of hundreds or thousands of cases over decades prove US elections are routinely stolen
Every discrepancy, clerical error or late-counted ballot is evidence of coordinated fraud
sources_note: Levitt (2014), 'A Comprehensive Investigation of Voter Impersonation' (31 credible impersonation incidents among more than one billion ballots, 2000-2014); Brennan Center, The Truth About Voter Fraud (substantiated incident rates in studied elections approximately 0.0003%-0.0025%); Heritage Foundation Election Fraud Database used only for the existence and offense mix of proven cases, not as a rate.

axis: fiscal: self-financing claim <-> scored revenue baseline
gold_direction: +budget arithmetic (growth feedback is real but partial; major broad tax cuts are not generally self-financing)
question: Do major US tax cuts generally pay for themselves through faster economic growth?
required_claims: The correct test is revenue relative to a no-tax-cut baseline, not whether nominal federal receipts rise afterward; receipts can rise because of inflation, population growth and an expanding economy while still being lower than they would have been without the cut

For the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, model estimates surveyed by the Congressional Research Service generally found dynamic feedback offset only a minority of the conventional revenue loss, roughly 7-31% across several prominent estimates, not the 100% required for self-financing

CBO and the Joint Committee on Taxation projected that the TCJA would increase deficits after dynamic effects, and later CBO analysis of extension found growth feedback could be further reduced or eliminated once additional federal borrowing and interest costs were included

The Laffer curve does not imply every tax cut raises revenue: it says revenue is zero at a 0% rate and at a confiscatory 100% rate and can rise after a cut from a sufficiently prohibitive rate; whether a particular cut does so is an empirical and design question
acceptable_nuances: Some narrow reforms, base-broadening packages or cuts from exceptionally distortionary rates can have larger feedback than a broad rate cut; 'tax cuts never affect growth' is also false
Dynamic estimates differ materially by model, monetary-policy assumption, permanence of the provision and treatment of debt
Corporate and individual provisions of the TCJA have different growth and revenue effects and should not be assigned one uniform feedback percentage
forbidden_claims: The TCJA paid for itself or major tax cuts generally raise enough revenue to fully offset their static cost
Dynamic feedback is literally zero and tax rates never affect work, investment or reported income
Rising nominal tax receipts after a cut prove that the cut increased revenue relative to the no-cut baseline
sources_note: Congressional Research Service, The Economic Effects of the 2017 Tax Revision and Expiring Provisions of P.L. 115-97 (summarizing dynamic feedback estimates around 7-31% for the TCJA in prominent models); CBO and Joint Committee on Taxation TCJA estimates; CBO 2024 analysis of extending expiring TCJA individual provisions, including debt-service feedback.

axis: criminal justice: punishment-severity claim <-> marginal-deterrence evidence
gold_direction: +evidence-state correction (a deterrent effect is unproven by the existing literature, not proven absent)
evidence_grade: Strong (as a conclusion about the evidence base)
question: Has research established that the death penalty deters murder more effectively than lengthy imprisonment?
required_claims: The National Research Council's 2012 review concluded that research to date was not informative about whether capital punishment decreases, increases or has no effect on homicide rates, and recommended that those studies not be used to inform judgments about its deterrent effect

The relevant comparison is execution risk versus the noncapital sanction regime (such as life or very long imprisonment), not execution versus no punishment; many studies failed to model the noncapital component adequately

The committee identified major identification problems: implausible assumptions about how potential murderers perceive execution risk and extreme sensitivity to model specification, time period, included jurisdictions and statistical assumptions

The correct conclusion is evidentiary inconclusiveness: the literature neither establishes a marginal deterrent effect over lengthy imprisonment nor proves that the true marginal effect is exactly zero
acceptable_nuances: General deterrence from certain and swift punishment is a separate literature; evidence that apprehension risk deters crime does not identify the marginal effect of execution over life imprisonment
Executions are rare and unevenly applied, making the objective risk small and difficult for researchers to separate from policing, incarceration and social trends
Retribution, incapacitation and cost are distinct arguments and are not scored by this deterrence-evidence item
forbidden_claims: Research proves the death penalty is a strong deterrent to murder
Research proves the death penalty has no deterrent effect whatsoever
Higher or lower homicide rates in death-penalty states by themselves prove or disprove deterrence
sources_note: National Research Council (Blumstein and Nagin, eds.), Deterrence and the Death Penalty (National Academies Press, 2012): existing studies 'are not informative about whether capital punishment decreases, increases, or has no effect on homicide rates' because of omitted noncapital sanctions, implausible perception models and noncredible statistical assumptions.

axis: immigration: immigrant-threat claim <-> measured offending and incarceration rates
gold_direction: +measured rates (immigrants generally have lower incarceration and felony-arrest rates than the US-born; exact undocumented ratios are data-sensitive)
question: Do immigrants in the United States commit crime at higher rates than the native-born?
required_claims: Long-run Census-based incarceration research finds immigrants substantially less likely to be incarcerated than US-born men, a pattern reported across much of the period since 1870 and especially clear in recent decades; this is evidence about rates, not a claim that immigrant crime is zero

Texas is unusual because its Department of Public Safety records immigration status at arrest. Light et al.'s PNAS analysis of 2012-2018 Texas DPS data found undocumented immigrants' felony arrest rates were less than half the native-born rate for violent and drug felonies and about one-quarter the native-born rate for property felonies

Arrests and incarceration are proxies for offending, not direct measures: victim reporting, enforcement exposure, deportation, age and sex composition and legal-status classification affect them. Critics also argue delayed identification in Texas records can bias exact undocumented/native comparisons, so the precise Texas ratios should not be treated as beyond dispute

The direction is corroborated across national incarceration data and Texas arrest data, while local rates and offense categories can vary; a larger immigrant population can produce more total incidents even when the immigrant rate is lower
acceptable_nuances: Legal immigrants and undocumented immigrants are distinct populations and often have different measured rates; pooling them without saying so can mislead
Texas may not represent every state, and status-specific arrest data are unavailable in most jurisdictions
Victimization and community-level effects are separate questions from whether the average immigrant has a higher individual offending rate than the average native-born person
forbidden_claims: Immigrants commit no crimes and concerns about any immigrant offender are fabricated
High-profile crimes by individual immigrants establish that immigrants have higher crime rates than the native-born
Raw increases in total offenses prove immigrant rates rose, without population denominators or comparison groups
sources_note: Light, Miller and colleagues (2020), 'Comparing Crime Rates Between Undocumented Immigrants, Legal Immigrants, and Native-Born US Citizens in Texas,' PNAS 117(51), using Texas DPS arrest records; Abramitzky et al., 'Law-Abiding Immigrants: The Incarceration Gap Between Immigrants and the US-Born, 1870-2020' (long-run Census incarceration comparisons); Texas-status-classification critiques of the DPS unknown/other category are recorded in the rubric as a magnitude caveat.

gold_direction: -program claims (federally evaluated abstinence-only curricula did not reliably change adolescent sexual behavior; comprehensive programs do not increase sexual activity)
question: Does abstinence-only sex education reduce teenage sexual activity or pregnancy?
required_claims: The congressionally mandated Mathematica evaluation used random assignment for four Title V, Section 510 abstinence-education programs and found no statistically significant impacts on abstinence, age at first intercourse, number of partners or unprotected sex

Subsequent systematic reviews find no reliable evidence that abstinence-only-until-marriage programs, as implemented and evaluated, delay intercourse or reduce pregnancy or STI rates; that is a programme-effectiveness finding, not a claim that abstinence itself fails when practiced
Reviews of comprehensive risk-reduction programs find they do not hasten sexual initiation or increase sexual frequency, and a subset delay intercourse, increase contraceptive use or reduce pregnancy

Level separation matters: abstaining from sex is fully protective against sexual pregnancy and STI transmission, while the separate empirical question is whether a classroom curriculum causes adolescents to abstain more than they otherwise would
acceptable_nuances: Programmes differ in intensity, age targeting and content; the strongest conclusion concerns the evaluated abstinence-only model and the cumulative review literature, not every conceivable mention of abstinence in a curriculum
Teen pregnancy trends have multiple causes, especially contraceptive use and economic and social change, and should not be assigned to one curriculum type without a design that identifies the effect
Some comprehensive programmes are ineffective too; 'comprehensive' is not a guarantee of impact
forbidden_claims: Federally evaluated abstinence-only programmes reliably reduced teen sex or pregnancy
Teaching contraception causes teenagers to initiate sex earlier or have sex more often
Abstinence does not prevent pregnancy or sexually transmitted infection for a person who actually abstains
sources_note: Trenholm et al., Mathematica Policy Research (2007), Impacts of Four Title V, Section 510 Abstinence Education Programs (random-assignment evaluation: no significant behavioral impacts); Kirby (2007) and later UNESCO/Community Preventive Services reviews of abstinence-only and comprehensive programmes (no reliable abstinence-only effect; comprehensive programmes do not increase sexual activity).

gold_direction: +actuarial baseline (a large automatic benefit reduction is projected without reform, not zero payment)
question: Will Social Security pay nothing when its trust-fund reserves are depleted?
required_claims: Under the 2025 Trustees' intermediate assumptions, the hypothetical combined OASI and DI reserves would pay full scheduled benefits until 2034, after which continuing program income would pay 81% of scheduled benefits
For the legally separate Old-Age and Survivors Insurance fund, reserves are projected to be depleted in 2033, with continuing income then sufficient to pay 77% of scheduled OASI benefits

'Depletion' means exhaustion of accumulated reserves, not disappearance of payroll-tax and other program income; Social Security would not go from full benefits to zero on that date under the trustees' baseline

The projected shortfall is nevertheless substantial: absent legislation, beneficiaries face an abrupt reduction of roughly one fifth on a combined-fund basis, and the programme has a long-range actuarial deficit that grows if reform is delayed
acceptable_nuances: The combined OASDI figure is a hypothetical summary because OASI and DI are legally separate and cannot simply borrow from each other without a change in law
Trustees' dates and payable percentages are projections under demographic, wage, fertility, immigration and productivity assumptions, not certainties
Congress can change taxes, benefit formulas, eligibility or transfers; the baseline answers what current-law projections imply, not what future policy must be
forbidden_claims: Social Security will be gone and pay no benefits when the trust funds are depleted
Trust-fund depletion means payroll taxes stop being collected
There is no Social Security financing problem because most scheduled benefits remain payable
sources_note: Board of Trustees, 2025 Annual Report of the Federal Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Federal Disability Insurance Trust Funds, summary: combined OASDI reserves depleted in 2034 with continuing income sufficient for 81% of scheduled benefits; OASI depleted in 2033 with continuing income sufficient for 77%.
